title: The First Letter of John
subtitle: Iōannou A, “First of John”
description: A letter with no greeting and no farewell, written by an old pastor to his “dear children” after a painful split in their church, so that those who stayed might know they have eternal life. It opens with the life that was heard, seen and touched with human hands, and returns again and again to three tests: what we believe about Jesus, whether we keep his commands, and whether we love one another. God is light; God is love; love has no room for fear; and we love because he loved us first. In the Open Word Bible, a new translation from the Greek given freely to the public domain, with an introduction to the letter’s shape and meaning and a conclusion on where to read next.

qa.question: What is the First Letter of John?
qa.answer: The twenty-third book of the New Testament, the longest of three letters that bear John’s name. It has no greeting or farewell and reads like a pastor’s sermon to a church he knows well. Written after a group had left the church denying that Jesus Christ had come in the flesh, it gives the believers who stayed ways to recognise the truth and to be sure of their standing with God. It states its own purpose in 5:13: so that you may know that you have eternal life.

qa.question: Who wrote 1 John, and when was it written?
qa.answer: The letter does not name its author. He writes as an eyewitness of Jesus and as a father to his readers, in language very close to the Gospel of John. From the second century the church received it as the work of John the apostle, writing late in life at Ephesus, probably in the last decades of the first century. Some scholars think it came from a leader in the circle that treasured John’s witness, perhaps the “elder” of 2 and 3 John.

qa.question: Why was 1 John written?
qa.answer: A group had left the church (“They went out from among us”, 2:19). They denied that Jesus is the Christ and would not confess him as one who has come in the flesh, while claiming to know God. The letter does not name them, and scholars debate whether they held the views later taught by Cerinthus or by those who said Christ only seemed to have a body. The writer reassures those who stayed and gives them tests of true faith: right belief about Jesus, obedience to his commands, and love for one another.

qa.question: What does “God is love” mean in 1 John?
qa.answer: The phrase occurs twice, in 4:8 and 4:16, alongside the earlier statement that “God is light” (1:5). The letter says love is found first not in our love for God but in his love for us, shown in sending his Son as the atoning sacrifice for our sins (4:10). Because God is love, anyone who knows him will love others, not in words only but in deeds (3:18), and love leaves no room for fear (4:18).

qa.question: Does 1 John teach that Christians do not sin?
qa.answer: It says both that anyone who claims to be free from sin is fooling themselves (1:8) and that whoever is born of God “does not go on sinning” (3:9). The tense of the Greek in chapter 3 describes a settled way of life rather than every single act. John Wesley drew on these verses for his teaching on Christian perfection; others read them as describing the direction of a believer’s life. All agree the letter calls Christians to holiness and promises forgiveness to those who confess their sins (1:9; 2:1–2).

qa.question: Which translation of the Bible is this?
qa.answer: The Open Word Bible, a new translation made directly from the Greek and dedicated to the public domain, printed here at its Balanced level, which aims to be accurate and to read naturally aloud. Like most modern Bibles it does not include the words about the Father, the Word and the Holy Spirit found in 5:7 of the King James Version, which are not in any early Greek manuscript. The reasoning behind each of its sentences, with the Greek beside it, is published at openwordbible.org. The introduction and conclusion were written for this edition.
